name: Hypochlorous acid lid spray

card.summary: A hypochlorous acid eyelid cleanser used for lid hygiene in blepharitis and redness; supporting data is small and mostly indirect.
card.aka: HOCl eyelid spray, lid hygiene spray
card.note: Hypochlorous acid solutions are unstable and lose potency over time; trials of lid hygiene broadly are small.

quick.overview:
Hypochlorous acid is a mild oxidising disinfectant that the body's white blood cells also make. Sprays and wipes based on it are sold for cleaning eyelids and lashes, and appearance-focused circles discuss them for lid redness and debris.

Research cited here covers blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction and Demodex mites more broadly. Direct trials of hypochlorous acid sprays for cosmetic eyelid redness were not found.
quick.mechanism: Hypochlorous acid kills microbes by oxidising their components. A 2017 study reported that a saline hygiene solution preserved with it reduced staphylococcal bacterial load on eyelid skin by more than 99% after 20 minutes.
quick.risks: The US EPA classifies the compound as non-hazardous, though as an oxidiser it can irritate depending on concentration and pH, and the solution loses strength quickly. Persistent lid redness has several possible causes, including meibomian gland dysfunction, rosacea and Demodex, that clinicians evaluate separately.

lead: Hypochlorous acid (HOCl) is a weak acid formed when chlorine dissolves in water, and it is the main disinfecting agent in chlorine solutions. White blood cells produce it naturally to fight microbes [1]. Commercial eyelid sprays and wipes use stabilised solutions for lid hygiene.

Lid hygiene is a standard element in managing blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD) and Demodex-related lid disease, where debris, bacteria and mites on the lid margins are implicated [2][3][4]. Reviews describe no gold-standard treatment for MGD but a range of options starting with conservative measures [3].
Published trials that specifically test hypochlorous acid sprays on cosmetic eyelid redness were not found; the available research addresses lid hygiene and blepharitis more generally.

paras: HOCl cannot be isolated as a pure compound and exists in equilibrium in water with hypochlorite and chlorine; at neutral pH solutions are roughly three-quarters HOCl. Light and certain metals accelerate its breakdown, and bottled solutions have short shelf lives [1].

By early 2016 the US FDA had cleared products with HOCl as the main active ingredient for wounds and infections, and it is also approved as a preservative for saline solutions. A 2017 study of an HOCl-preserved saline hygiene solution reported over 99% reduction in staphylococcal load on eyelid skin after 20 minutes without changing bacterial diversity [1].

Dry eye disease is subdivided into aqueous-deficient and evaporative forms, and MGD is the leading cause of the evaporative type [5][3]. Demodex mites were found in a high proportion of eyelashes with cylindrical dandruff in a 2005 study, and a systematic review has examined treatments for Demodex blepharitis [6][7]. Tea tree oil lid scrubs have been reported in a small retrospective series [8].
Rosacea, which affects eyelids as well as skin, is covered by a global consensus treatment update [9].

The US EPA classifies HOCl as non-hazardous, and a clinical test cited in an encyclopedic source found HOCl water non-irritating to eye and skin. As an oxidiser it can irritate depending on concentration and pH, and listed hazard statements include eye and respiratory irritation [1].

Registered studies include a trial comparing a tea-tree-based lid cleanser with another lid hygiene product in blepharitis [10], a comparison of thermal pulsation with a standard lid hygiene regime [11], a trial of long-term treatment for MGD and dry eye [12], and trials of povidone-iodine for blepharitis [13]. No studies found tested hypochlorous acid sprays specifically for cosmetic eyelid redness.
